name: event-driven
context: Asynchronous communication between decoupled services where producers emit events when state changes occur, and consumers react to those events independently
benefits: Scalability: Services scale independently based on event load
Agility: Add new consumers without modifying producers
Resilience: Event buffer accommodates surges; consumers can fail and recover
Loose Coupling: Services only know about the event router
Auditability: Complete event log for debugging and compliance
Real-time processing: Consumers can respond to events immediately as they occur
Independent deployment: Producers and consumers are deployed independently
tradeoffs: Eventual Consistency: Consumers may have stale data temporarily
Debugging Complexity: Distributed tracing required to follow event flows
Schema Evolution: Breaking changes require versioning strategies
Idempotency: Consumers must handle duplicate events gracefully
Operational complexity: Requires monitoring consumer lag, DLQs, and event processing
Initial learning curve: EDA requires strong domain modeling skills
use_cases: Multiple services reacting to same data (order placed triggers shipping, inventory, analytics)
Building microservices ecosystem with independent scaling
IoT or sensor data ingestion (high-volume, asynchronous streams)
Audit trail and compliance requirements (event replay)
avoid_when: Simple CRUD operations with synchronous response expectations
Strong consistency requirements where immediate confirmation is needed
Small teams lacking distributed systems experience
Projects with fixed, predictable data volumes
component_types: Event Producer: Emits events when state changes occur
Event Channel: Message broker that routes events from producers to consumers
Event Consumer: Subscribes to and processes events asynchronously
Event Schema Registry: Centralized storage for event schema definitions
Dead Letter Queue: Captures failed events for later inspection and retry
Correlation ID: Enables distributed tracing across event flows
design_principles: Decoupling: Producers and consumers are independent; event router acts as intermediary
Async Communication: Services communicate via events, not requests; message brokers handle event delivery
Event Propagation: State changes propagate to all interested consumers via pub/sub or fan-out patterns
Temporal Decoupling: Producers and consumers don't need to be online simultaneously; message retention in broker
Schema as Contract: Treat event schemas as long-term contracts; version carefully with additive evolution
Idempotency: Consumers must handle duplicate events gracefully using event IDs and upserts
best_practices: Schema Design: Design events as products not side effects; use richer events over many tiny ones; version via additive evolution only
Event Envelope: Wrap every event with standard envelope containing eventId, correlationId, timestamp, and schemaVersion
Idempotent Consumers: Store processed eventId values to skip duplicates; use upserts or conditional writes for database operations
Dead Letter Queues: Implement DLQs for every consumer with alerting; never let a poison message block the pipeline
Retry with Backoff: Configure retry mechanisms with exponential backoff (typically 3-5 attempts)
Distributed Tracing: Implement correlation IDs end-to-end; use OpenTelemetry for granular insights across event flows
Consumer Lag Monitoring: Monitor lag as primary health signal (lag > 10,000 events for 5 minutes triggers alerts)
Event SLOs: Set SLOs for maximum acceptable lag (e.g., 5 seconds at 99th percentile)
Event Granularity: Represent business-relevant transitions; don't force consumers to listen to five events to understand one action
Choreography vs Orchestration: Use choreography for simple independent reactions; orchestration for business-critical workflows with compensation steps
